summary: The build can start: Python, node/npx, Docker, az (signed in), the documentdb MCP server, and the Microsoft Learn docs search are available and the DocumentDB agent skills needed for development are installed. Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated (they described Cosmos DB, older naming, or other products) and must be corrected before coding. Missing developer accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and a few CLI tools (mongosh, optional infra CLIs) would speed development or local verification but are not blocking; there are clear workarounds.
summary_points: Essential runtime and verification tools for this sample (python, pip, pymongo use, node/npx, docker, az signed-in, and the documentdb MCP server) are present so the developer can implement and verify the sample against the live cluster.

Multiple cold answers are incorrect because they describe the Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb / RU-based) model rather than the vCore-based Azure DocumentDB product (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters); the builder must use mongoClusters and the az documentdb CLI group.

Vector and full-text features are supported natively but use DocumentDB-specific commands and operators (createIndexes / cosmosSearch and createSearchIndexes + $search), not the community-style knnVector or Cosmos RU connection patterns the cold answers suggested.
Local development can use the provided DocumentDB local gateway Docker image (gateway on port 10260); the cold answer claiming no emulator was available is wrong.
Microsoft Entra ID (AAD / OIDC) authentication is supported and must be handled via the documented OIDC callback/token path; a cold answer that said AAD is not supported is wrong.

Accelerator missing: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — helpful but not blocking. mongosh is not on PATH and would make manual verification easier; the documentdb MCP server provides alternatives.

tools.needed_for: Run the sample app, create venv, install deps (pymongo, llama-index, embedding/LLM clients), run ingestion and query scripts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Sample cannot be executed locally; builder cannot run ingestion, embedding, or LlamaIndex code.
tools.workaround: Install Python and re-run; in a pinch run code in a container with the same Python version.

tools.needed_for: Install Python packages (pymongo, llama-index, llama-index vector-store, embedding/LLM clients).

tools.workaround: Use a docker image with dependencies preinstalled; or ensure pip is installed via package manager.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server
tools.needed_for: Data-plane verification: list databases, inspect collections and indexes, create vector and search indexes, run aggregation pipelines and explain plans against the live cluster.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server present in inventory with tools such as documentdb_create_index, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_aggregate etc.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to inspect and verify index creation and query plans programmatically; the developer would need mongosh or portal-based steps.
tools.workaround: Use Azure portal and manual mongosh (if installed) to inspect indexes and run queries.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn docs search and fetch)
tools.needed_for: Ground facts, examples, and command-line syntax for DocumentDB, vector search, full-text search, auth modes, Bicep/Terraform resource types.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to reliably verify up-to-date service recommendations and API shapes.
tools.workaround: Manually use docs.microsoft.com in a browser.

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search skill
tools.needed_for: Guidance on creating and tuning vector indexes (DiskANN / HNSW / IVF), choosing dims, and running $search + cosmosSearch queries.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to choose index algorithm and parameters for the sample's dataset; suboptimal index choices could lead to poor recall/latency.
tools.workaround: Follow the general documents in the Microsoft docs on vector-search and use conservative defaults (DiskANN or HNSW on M30+).

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment skill
tools.needed_for: Instructions and best practices to run the open-source DocumentDB gateway locally (Docker image, port 10260, TLS config) for development and integration tests.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder might mistakenly believe a local gateway is unavailable and attempt to develop only against the live cluster; slower iteration and higher cost.
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster for testing (the environment already provides a cluster), or rely on Docker-based local setup instructions in the docs.

tools.name: documentdb-driver skill
tools.needed_for: Driver usage best-practices (singleton MongoClient, connection pooling, OIDC callback for AAD tokens), which the sample must apply for production-like examples (serverless / web frameworks).
tools.impact_if_missing: The sample may create inefficient code patterns (creating new MongoClient per request) and encounter connection limits in serverless demos.
tools.workaround: Follow pymongo official docs for singleton use; use the skill later for tuning.

tools.name: documentdb-connection skill
tools.needed_for: Connection tuning (timeouts, pools) and OIDC token integration patterns for Python applications; useful for LlamaIndex/LLM multi-threaded apps.
tools.impact_if_missing: Connection errors or pool exhaustion in tests, especially under load.
tools.workaround: Use pymongo docs and recommended defaults; keep a single shared client for the process.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (use the Cosmos DB account resource with Kind set to MongoDB for a Mongo-compatible DocumentDB cluster).
confusions.grounded_answer: The cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource provider Microsoft.DocumentDB). Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore-based Azure DocumentDB clusters.
confusions.grounding_source: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared resource provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical overlap: Cosmos DB accounts use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; older guidance for Cosmos DB Mongo API uses databaseAccounts which is different from the vCore-managed mongoClusters resource.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses databaseAccounts resource type, any Bicep/Terraform that creates a 'databaseAccounts' will target Cosmos DB account semantics (RU model) instead of the vCore-based mongoClusters; provisioning or management calls will fail or create the wrong resource.
improvements: Update Quickstart and Bicep samples to highlight 'mongoClusters' for vCore clusters and include a short note 'use mongoClusters not databaseAccounts for Azure DocumentDB (vCore)' on the databaseAccounts page.
Add a prominent deprecation / clarify note on older 'databaseAccounts' pages that they refer to Cosmos DB account models, not the vCore mongoClusters resource.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group 'az cosmosdb'. e.g. az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. (az cosmosdb is part of the core az CLI, not a separate extension.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the 'az documentdb' CLI group; cluster create/list/show/update commands are under az documentdb mongocluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create).
confusions.grounding_source: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Overlapping product names and historically 'cosmosdb' CLI group managed Mongo API accounts; new vCore-managed service exposes its own az documentdb command group.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb for CLI examples will target Cosmos DB accounts and not the vCore mongoClusters resource; commands will be incorrect or fail for the target service.
improvements: In CLI quickstarts, change the example command group from 'az cosmosdb' to 'az documentdb mongocluster' and add a note explaining the difference.
Add a short 'Which CLI group to use' note on the service overview page directing developers to az documentdb for mongoClusters.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' with properties.apiProperties.kind or kind: 'MongoDB'. Example: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: accountName; kind: 'MongoDB'; properties: { consistencyPolicy: {...} } }. Terraform (azurerm): use azurerm_cosmosdb_account (set offer_type/api_kind to MongoDB) and azureRM provider resources like azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database for DBs/collections.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource types for vCore DocumentDB clusters (Bicep/Terraform AzAPI support). databaseAccounts is for Cosmos DB account models (RU-based). For vCore clusters the templates and AzAPI resource name is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace and earlier Cosmos DB-based Mongo API examples use databaseAccounts; the new vCore-based cluster resource uses a separate child resource name (mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts in Bicep/Terraform will produce a Cosmos DB account (RU-model), not a vCore mongoClusters cluster; automated IaC in the sample would be wrong.
improvements: Add explicit example Bicep snippet showing Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in the sample repo README and add a short note in the 'Create cluster' quickstart clarifying which resource type to use for vCore clusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a MongoDB connection string. Example (Cosmos Mongo API style): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. For SRV style you may see mongodb+srv://<username>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<db>?authSource=admin&tls=true. Port for TLS is 10255 (Cosmos Mongo API); options must include SSL/TLS (ssl=true or tls=true), authSource=admin (or as provided), and replicaSet=globaldb for Cosmos Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Connection strings are provided by the cluster's connection-strings API and typically look like mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<clusterName>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/ (SRV style) or mongodb://<user>:<password>@<clusterHost>/ with TLS enabled. DocumentDB clusters use their own host suffix and support SCRAM-SHA-256 and OIDC (MONGODB-OIDC) auth flows; do not assume Cosmos DB RU endpoints (10255) or replicaSet=globaldb.
confusions.grounding_source: Get cluster connection strings and Quickstart Python examples

grounding_links.title: Get connection strings for a DocumentDB cluster (CLI/portal)
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python (connection example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's older Mongo endpoint patterns (account.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255) rather than the vCore DocumentDB cluster SRV / global.mongocluster hostnames and the OIDC options the service also supports.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB Mongo API connection string examples (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding the wrong host suffix or port (10255) or assuming replicaSet=globaldb will cause connection errors; the sample must read DOCUMENTDB_URI and use whatever connection string the cluster provides.
improvements: Emphasize in the quickstart and samples: read the cluster's connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and do not hardcode ports or host suffixes.
Add example connection strings for both SRV and non-SRV forms on the cluster's connection-strings docs page.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as Cosmos-style Request Units (RUs) for provisioned throughput (manual or autoscale). There is also a serverless option for small workloads on supported APIs. Traditional vCore-based tiers (as used by managed MongoDB/vCore offerings) do not apply when you use the Mongo-compatible Cosmos DB account model.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is billed by compute tiers (vCores) plus storage. You pick a cluster tier (M10/M20/M30/etc.) and storage per shard; there are no RU charges. This differs from Cosmos DB RU-model accounts.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the Cosmos DB RU/throughput model rather than the vCore-based Azure DocumentDB pricing model; the services share naming and provider namespace so they're easy to confuse.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB provisioning and RU docs

confusions.build_risk: Choosing the wrong capacity abstraction (RUs vs vCores) would lead the sample to create incorrect indexes or to document the wrong scaling instructions. For example, vector index sizing guidance (recommended by DocumentDB skills) depends on cluster tier.
improvements: Add a short 'Billing model' paragraph in every quickstart that creates or references cluster resources, explaining vCore tiers for DocumentDB and RUs for Cosmos DB.
Add a note in the sample README that the provided cluster in the run environment is vCore-based and specify the exact tier used (M30 in skill_md).

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: The Mongo-compatible endpoint uses standard Mongo auth (SCRAM username/password / database credentials). X.509 certificate auth may be supported in some managed offerings, but Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is NOT supported for the Mongo DB wire endpoint in typical Cosmos DB Mongo API deployments — you authenticate with the Mongo user and password (SCRAM). There is no driver-side AAD token flow for Mongo endpoints; use the provided Mongo credentials or certificate methods where supported.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native SCRAM username/password authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication. When Entra ID is enabled on the cluster, drivers can connect using MONGODB-OIDC with an OIDC callback or token (the docs show a Python example using azure-identity + a pymongo OIDC callback). Entra ID must be enabled in cluster authConfig.allowedModes.
confusions.grounding_source: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
How to build Python console app (OIDC example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected older Cosmos DB Mongo API restrictions or other managed offerings where AAD/OIDC was not implemented; DocumentDB (vCore) supports Entra ID via OIDC when enabled.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes only SCRAM auth, it will omit the documented OIDC callback flow and miss Entra ID examples required by secure production setups; code demonstrating OIDC integration will be missing or incorrect.
improvements: Add an 'Authentication options' section to quickstarts showing both SCRAM and Microsoft Entra ID (with a short Python example using DefaultAzureCredential and the pymongo OIDC callback).
Ensure the sample's README describes how to enable Entra ID on the cluster (authConfig.allowedModes) and links to the OIDC example.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., pymongo for Python, the official Node.js MongoDB driver). There is no separate service-specific Mongo client; do NOT use azure-cosmos SDK for Mongo wire traffic. Use pymongo.MongoClient pointed at the provided connection string.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python). The quickstart uses pymongo and shows sample code; LlamaIndex or other vector-store integrations use existing drivers to access the cluster.
confusions.grounding_source: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Index implementations available on the managed service include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN (service supports HNSW/IVF/DiskANN-backed vector indexes). Example Mongo-style createIndex I would use: db.transcripts.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', spaceType: 'cosine', dims: 1536, efConstruction: 200 } } ).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index types DiskANN, HNSW, and IVF. Index creation uses the DocumentDB-specific createIndexes / createIndex runCommand shape with cosmosSearch / cosmosSearchOptions (e.g., createIndexes with key: { path: 'embedding', kind: 'cosmosSearch' } and cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' and their tuning parameters). The MongoDB community 'knnVector' syntax is not the documented command for DocumentDB.
confusions.grounding_source: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search docs)

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB - vector-search
Create a DiskANN/IVF/HNSW index examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a community MongoDB-style knnVector createIndex example (MongoDB 7+ syntax) rather than the DocumentDB-specific createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions index-definition shape.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the knnVector createIndex form, the index creation will fail against DocumentDB; the sample must create the DocumentDB-specific vector index using createIndexes with cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions.
improvements: Add a short example 'how to create a vector index' to the quickstart that copies the exact createIndexes JSON used by DocumentDB for HNSW/IVF/DiskANN.
Include an example LlamaIndex/LLM integration that shows the index creation step and the exact parameters used for the sample embedding dimension.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text: either use the Mongo text index for simple text search or integrate the cluster with Azure Cognitive Search for richer full-text and cognitive indexing. Hybrid vector+text search is typically implemented by using the vector index for nearest-neighbor retrieval and combining it with text scoring (either via application-side re-ranking or an Azure Cognitive Search pipeline). There isn't a single proprietary hybrid search API — you combine vector knn retrieval and text filters/scores.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides integrated full-text search (BM25) via createSearchIndexes + $search and supports hybrid (BM25 + vector) retrieval on the same collection. Hybrid search is implemented inside DocumentDB by running separate keyword and vector queries and fusing results (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) either on the server side ($unionWith) or client side. You do not need Azure Cognitive Search for hybrid search on DocumentDB.
confusions.grounding_source: Full-text search and Hybrid search docs

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed use of external Azure Cognitive Search or the older MongoDB text index; DocumentDB exposes a built-in BM25 engine and server-side fusion capability.

confusion_sources.title: Using Azure Cognitive Search with Cosmos DB (different service guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample externalizes full-text search to Cognitive Search, it will complicate the demo and misrepresent the integrated DocumentDB capabilities; this would add cost and architecture changes that are unnecessary.
improvements: Add an example in the RAG sample README demonstrating creating a search index with createSearchIndexes and one example of server-side Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
Document that Azure Cognitive Search is not required for BM25 or hybrid search in DocumentDB.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Targeted Mongo wire protocol support is MongoDB 6.x/7.0 era (many managed Mongo-compatible offerings advertise MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol). However, not all server-side MongoDB features are available: server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, some aggregation or change-stream behaviors, and operations that rely on underlying Mongo storage-engine internals may be unsupported or behave differently. Expect differences in transactions, server-side plugins, and some admin/replica-set commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports multiple MongoDB wire protocol versions (notably 5.0 through 8.0) and implements broad MQL compatibility (the service claims ~99.03% operator coverage). Some administrative commands and server-side extensions are not available because the service runs the DocumentDB engine, not MongoDB server. The exact operator compatibility list is documented in the compatibility reference.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was vague and didn't list the supported wire-protocol range; DocumentDB explicitly documents supported versions and operator coverage.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming only a single MongoDB version could cause the builder to pick incompatible driver features or fail to test version features (e.g., using a driver feature introduced in a wire protocol version the cluster doesn't advertise).
improvements: Add a small 'Supported Mongo wire protocol versions' note to the service overview quickstart (e.g., 'DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0 through 8.0').

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full-featured local emulator for the Mongo-compatible vector-enabled managed service. For local development use the official MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7.0) listening on 27017 for basic protocol compatibility, but vector/indexing features from the managed service will not be available locally. If you must test management or index features, run them against the live cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is a DocumentDB local (gateway) Docker image and an Azure Local / operator-based local evaluation path. The gateway listens on port 10260 by default (tls) and the docs show how to run ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local and connect via mongodb://localhost:10260 with TLS and tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for local dev/eval.
confusions.grounding_source: Quickstart: Development loop and local gateway documentation

grounding_links.title: Development loop (DocumentDB local gateway, port 10260)
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed no official local gateway existed and recommended using generic mongo images; in fact DocumentDB publishes an official local gateway image and quickstarts.

confusion_sources.title: Using mongo docker for generic protocol tests (tutorial)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no local gateway, they'll miss the faster developer iteration using the local gateway image and either over-use the live cluster (costly) or write inaccurate integration tests.
improvements: Add a clear 'Local development' section to the sample README pointing to the documentdb local gateway Docker example and the default port (10260).
Document that vector/index features are available via the local gateway for evaluation (with appropriate TLS caveats).

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams support depends on the managed Mongo API: historically Cosmos DB exposed a different change feed rather than Mongo change streams. For many Cosmos Mongo API deployments: Mongo change streams are not supported; instead use the Cosmos DB change feed or service-specific change mechanisms. If the service offers change streams, you may need to enable the feature or use a supported server version. (Treat change streams as likely unavailable unless explicitly documented for your cluster.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams (including multi-shard change streams in preview). Change streams must be enabled if necessary for certain multi-shard modes or preview features; the docs explain how to enable/verify and list limitations (resume tokens, multi-shard ordering caveats).

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer reflected older differences in Cosmos DB's Mongo API; DocumentDB (vCore) has its own change-stream implementation and preview features for multi-shard streams.

confusion_sources.title: Change streams in Azure Cosmos DB's API for MongoDB (different product guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample relies on change streams and the builder assumes they're unsupported, they may choose an offline or polling approach and miss a more efficient real-time design; conversely, assuming change streams without enabling the feature could cause runtime errors.
improvements: Add a short 'Change streams' note in the sample README: describe when to enable them on the cluster and link to the docs with the example 'db.collection.watch()' usage.
Document multi-shard limitations explicitly (ordering, resumability caveats).

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server to get data-plane tooling appropriate for the DocumentDB/Mongo-compatible cluster. The general azure MCP server covers Azure resource provisioning but the documentdb MCP server provides collection/index inspection and query-plan tools specifically for this service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides the data-plane tools (list databases, create/list/drop indexes, run queries, explain). The general 'azure' MCP server covers control-plane provisioning and docs lookups.
confusions.grounding_source: Machine inventory (documentdb MCP server present) and docs

grounding_links.title: documentdb (MCP server) - inventory

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft used the name 'Azure DocumentDB' as the original document database service; that platform evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The Azure DocumentDB name is legacy; Azure Cosmos DB is the umbrella service. The open-source 'DocumentDB' projects are distinct and unrelated — Microsoft’s DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is a managed Microsoft service with its own engine and compatibility layers.
confusions.grounded_answer: The answer is accurate for context: the vCore offering was previously named 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and was rebranded 'Azure DocumentDB' (with MongoDB compatibility). The service is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) which is distinct from the original 2014-2017 DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB evolution; the docs explicitly clarify the lineage.

grounding_links.title: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB? (FAQ)
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The Mongo-compatible endpoint sits on the provider's managed DocumentDB/Cosmos DB engine (a Mongo wire compatibility layer over the service engine). In practice you use MongoDB drivers and most app code will be unchanged, but expect differences in billing (RUs), some unsupported server-side features, and subtle differences in query semantics and performance characteristics.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the service uses the DocumentDB engine (open-source) with a MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility layer. Applications use standard MongoDB drivers; most app code is unchanged, but differences exist in admin commands and a small set of supported operators—documented in the compatibility guide.

confusions.question: What collection and index will the sample create for transcripts and vectors?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a collection named 'transcripts'. Create a vector index on the 'embedding' field. Example command I would run: db.transcripts.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', spaceType: 'cosine', dims: 1536, efConstruction: 200 } } ).
confusions.grounded_answer: The collection naming (e.g., 'transcripts') is reasonable, and DocumentDB requires embeddings as number[] stored in a field (embedding). However, createIndex must use DocumentDB's createIndexes / cosmosSearchOptions shape (e.g., use createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind: 'vector-hnsw'/'vector-ivf'/'vector-diskann' and dims). The community 'knnVector' createIndex form is not the documented API for DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB - index creation examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used generic MongoDB 7.0 knnVector syntax common in other MongoDB distributions rather than the DocumentDB-specific createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions format.
confusions.build_risk: Running a knnVector createIndex will fail against DocumentDB; the builder must create the DocumentDB-specific vector index shape or use the sample's MCP/index APIs.
improvements: Provide an exact createIndexes JSON sample in the RAG sample README that creates the vector index with cosmosSearchOptions and dims matching the chosen embedding model.

confusions.question: What query/aggregation will the sample use to retrieve nearest neighbour chunks for a query embedding?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the service's vector search aggregation stage. Example aggregation I would attempt: db.transcripts.aggregate([ { $search: { knnBeta: { vector: <queryVec>, path: 'embedding', k: 10 } } }, { $project: { score: { $meta: 'searchScore' }, text: 1, source: 1, timestamp: 1 } } ]). Then re-rank or trim results to fit the LLM context window and attach citations (source + timestamp) for each chunk.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use $search with the DocumentDB cosmosSearch operator, e.g. db.collection.aggregate([{ $search: { cosmosSearch: { vector: <queryVec>, path: 'embedding', k: 10 } } }, { $project: { score: { $meta: 'searchScore' }, text: 1, source:1, timestamp:1 } }]). The cold answer's knnBeta form is not the documented variant; use cosmosSearch element.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB - perform a vector search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used knnBeta / knn-like syntax not aligned with DocumentDB's documented cosmosSearch operator.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong aggregation operator will produce runtime errors. The sample must use cosmosSearch in $search for vector retrieval, then $project $meta: 'searchScore' to get ranking.
improvements: Add exact aggregation examples using $search + cosmosSearch in the sample README and show $project retrieving { $meta: 'searchScore' } along with text/source metadata.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model selection and output dimension
information_gaps.description: The prompt does not specify which embedding model (provider and model name) to use or the output dimensionality. The DocumentDB vector index must be created with a matching 'dims' parameter. I searched Microsoft Learn docs and the installed skills for advice and found index-dimension limits and guidance, but nothing that picks a concrete model/dimension for this sample. The builder must pick and document the embedding model and set the vector index dims accordingly.

information_gaps.title: LLM model and provider choice
information_gaps.description: The prompt leaves the LLM (for answer synthesis) unspecified. The builder needs to decide a provider and model (OpenAI/Azure OpenAI or local LLM) and document credentials and env vars. I reviewed the prompt_review and skills for best-practice guidance but no single canonical choice is enforced; this remains a builder decision.

information_gaps.title: Sample earnings-call PDFs and licensing
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks to ingest earnings-call PDFs but does not include a sample transcript or specify a public data source/license. I searched the quickstarts and skills and found no bundled sample. The builder must supply or document sample PDFs (with appropriate license) or provide a script that accepts user-supplied PDFs.

information_gaps.title: Idempotent seed script and record deduplication
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires ingesting documents and creating indexes but does not require an idempotent seed script. The skills and docs explain insert/bulk operations but don't provide a canonical, idempotent sample ingestion pattern that detects and skips already-ingested chunks. The builder must choose a chunk_id scheme and implement dedupe explicitly.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on the developer machine to run ad-hoc queries, inspect indexes and test aggregation pipelines locally against the cluster. Install from MongoDB's official distributions (or package manager) and use it with --tlsAllowInvalidCertificates when connecting to local gateway for dev. If not added, rely on the documentdb MCP server for index and query inspection.
